{{Short description|Mathematical formal infinite series}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Hahn series''' (sometimes also known as '''Hahn–Mal'cev–Neumann series''') are a type of [[formal series|formal infinite series]]. They are a generalization of [[Puiseux series]] (themselves a generalization of [[formal power series]]) and were first introduced by [[Hans Hahn (mathematician)|Hans Hahn]] in 1907<ref>Hahn (1907)</ref> (and then further generalized by [[Anatoly Maltsev]] and [[Bernhard Neumann]] to a non-commutative setting). They allow for arbitrary exponents of the [[Indeterminate (variable)|indeterminate]] so long as the set supporting them forms a [[well-order]]ed subset of the [[Valuation (algebra)|value group]] (typically <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> or <math>\mathbb{R}</math>). Hahn series were first introduced, as groups, in the course of the [[mathematical proof|proof]] of the [[Hahn embedding theorem]] and then studied by him in relation to [[Hilbert's second problem]].

==Formulation==
The [[field (mathematics)|field]] of Hahn series <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> (in the indeterminate <math>T</math>) over a field <math>K</math> and with value group <math>\Gamma</math> (an ordered group) is the set of formal expressions of the form

:<math>f = \sum_{e\in\Gamma} c_e T^e</math>

with <math>c_e \in K</math> such that the support <math>\operatorname{supp} f:=\{ e\in \Gamma : c_e \neq 0 \}</math> of ''f'' is [[well-order]]ed. The sum and product of

:<math>f = \sum_{e\in\Gamma} c_e T^e</math> and <math>g = \sum_{e\in\Gamma} d_e T^e</math>

are given by

:<math>f+g = \sum_{e\in\Gamma} (c_e+d_e) T^e</math>
and
:<math>fg = \sum_{e\in\Gamma} \left(\sum_{e'+e''=e} c_{e'} d_{e''}\right) T^e</math>

(in the latter, the sum <math>\sum_{e'+e''=e}</math> over values <math>(e',e'')</math> such that <math>c_{e'} \neq 0</math>, <math>d_{e''} \neq 0</math> and <math>e'+e''=e</math> is finite because a well-ordered set cannot contain an infinite decreasing sequence).<ref>Neumann (1949), Lemmas (3.2) and (3.3)</ref>

For example, <math>T^{-1/p} + T^{-1/p^2} + T^{-1/p^3} + \cdots</math> is a Hahn series (over any field) because the set of [[rational number|rationals]]
:<math>\left\{-\frac{1}{p}, -\frac{1}{p^2}, -\frac{1}{p^3}, \ldots\right\}</math>
is well-ordered; it is not a [[Puiseux series]] because the denominators in the exponents are unbounded. (And if the base field ''K'' has [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] ''p'', then this Hahn series satisfies the equation <math>X^p-X = T^{-1}</math> so it is algebraic over <math>K(T)</math>.)

==Properties==

=== Properties of the valued field ===

The valuation <math>v(f)</math> of a non-zero Hahn series

:<math>f = \sum_{e\in\Gamma} c_e T^e</math>

is defined as the smallest <math>e \in \Gamma</math> such that <math>c_e \neq 0</math> (in other words, the smallest element of the support of <math>f</math>): this makes <math>K[[T^\Gamma]]</math> into a [[Spherically complete field|spherically complete]] [[valuation (algebra)|valued field]] with value group <math>\Gamma</math> and residue field <math>K</math> (justifying ''a posteriori'' the terminology). In fact, if <math>K</math> has characteristic zero, then <math>(K[[T^{\Gamma}]],v)</math> is [[up to]] (non-unique) [[isomorphism]] the only spherically complete valued field with residue field <math>K</math> and value group <math>\Gamma</math>.<ref>Kaplansky, Irving, ''Maximal fields with valuation'', Duke Mathematical Journal, vol. 1, n°2, 1942.</ref>
The valuation <math>v</math> defines a [[topological space|topology]] on <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>. If <math>\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{R}</math>, then <math>v</math> corresponds to an [[Ultrametric space|ultrametric]] absolute value <math>|f| = \exp(-v(f))</math>, with respect to which <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> is a [[complete metric space]]. However, unlike in the case of [[formal Laurent series]] or Puiseux series, the formal sums used in defining the elements of the field do ''not'' converge: in the case of <math>T^{-1/p} + T^{-1/p^2} + T^{-1/p^3} + \cdots</math> for example, the absolute values of the terms tend to 1 (because their valuations tend to 0), so the series is not convergent (such series are sometimes known as "pseudo-convergent"<ref>Kaplansky (1942, ''Duke Math. J.'', definition on p.&nbsp;303)</ref>).

=== Algebraic properties ===

If <math>K</math> is [[algebraically closed field|algebraically closed]] (but not necessarily of characteristic zero) and <math>\Gamma</math> is [[divisible group|divisible]], then <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> is algebraically closed.<ref>MacLane (1939, ''Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.'', theorem 1 (p.&nbsp;889))</ref> Thus, the [[algebraic closure]] of <math>K((T))</math> is contained in <math>\overline{K}[[T^{\mathbb{Q}}]]</math>, where <math>\overline{K}</math> is the algebraic closure of <math>K</math> (when <math>K</math> is of characteristic zero, it is exactly the field of [[Puiseux series]]): in fact, it is possible to give a somewhat analogous description of the algebraic closure of <math>K((T))</math> in positive characteristic as a subset of <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>.<ref>Kedlaya (2001, ''Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.'')</ref>

If <math>K</math> is an [[ordered field]] then <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> is totally ordered by making the indeterminate <math>T</math> infinitesimal (greater than 0 but less than any positive element of <math>K</math>) or, equivalently, by using the [[lexicographic order]] on the coefficients of the series. If <math>K</math> is [[real closed field|real-closed]] and <math>\Gamma</math> is divisible then <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> is itself real-closed.<ref>Alling (1987, §6.23, (2) (p.&nbsp;218))</ref> This fact can be used to analyse (or even construct) the field of [[surreal number]]s (which is isomorphic, as an ordered field, to the field of Hahn series with [[real number|real]] coefficients and value group the surreal numbers themselves<ref>Alling (1987, theorem of §6.55 (p.&nbsp;246))</ref>).

If ''κ'' is an infinite [[regular cardinal]], one can consider the subset of <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> consisting of series whose support set <math>\{ e\in \Gamma : c_e \neq 0 \}</math> has [[cardinality]] (strictly) less than ''κ'': it turns out that this is also a field, with much the same algebraic closedness properties as the full <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>: e.g., it is algebraically closed or real closed when <math>K</math> is so and <math>\Gamma</math> is divisible.<ref>Alling (1987, §6.23, (3) and (4) (pp.&nbsp;218–219))</ref>

== Summable families ==

=== Summable families ===

One can define a notion of summable families in <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>. If <math>I</math> is a set and <math>(f_i)_{i \in I}</math> is a family of Hahn series <math>f_i \in K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>, then we say that <math>(f_i)_{i \in I}</math> is summable if the set <math>\bigcup \limits_{i \in I} \operatorname{supp} f_i \subset \Gamma</math> is well-ordered, and each set <math>\{i \in I \mid e \in \operatorname{supp} f_i\}</math> for <math>e \in \Gamma</math> is finite.

We may then define the sum <math>\sum \limits_{i \in I} f_i</math> as the Hahn series

:<math>\sum_{i \in I} f_i := \sum \limits_{e \in \Gamma} \left(\sum_{i \in I} f_i(e)\right) T^e.</math>

If <math>(f_i)_{i \in I},(g_i)_{i \in I}</math> are summable, then so are the families <math>(f_i+g_i)_{i \in I},(f_i g_j)_{(i,j) \in I \times I}</math>, and we have<ref>Joris van der Hoeven</ref>

:<math>\sum_{i \in I} f_i+g_i=\sum_{i \in I} f_i+\sum_{i \in I} g_i</math>
and
:<math>\sum_{(i,j) \in I \times I} f_i g_j = \left(\sum_{i \in I} f_i\right)\left(\sum_{i \in I} g_i\right).</math>

This notion of summable family does not correspond to the notion of convergence in the valuation topology on <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>. For instance, in <math>\mathbb{Q}\left[\left[T^\mathbb{Q}\right]\right]</math>, the family <math>(T^{\frac{n}{n+1}}+T^{n+1})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> is summable but the sequence <math>\big(\sum \limits_{k \leq n} T^{\frac{k}{k+1}}+T^{k+1}\big)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> does not converge.

=== Evaluating analytic functions ===

Let <math>a \in \mathbb{R}</math> and let <math>\mathcal{A}_a</math> denote the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of real-valued [[function (mathematics)|functions]] which are [[analytic function|analytic]] on a [[neighborhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] of <math>a</math>.

If <math>K</math> contains <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, then we can evaluate every element <math>f</math> of <math>\mathcal{A}_a</math> at every element of <math>K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math> of the form <math>a+\varepsilon</math>, where the valuation of <math>\varepsilon</math> is strictly positive. 
Indeed, the family <math>\bigg(\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}\varepsilon^n\bigg)_{\!n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> is always summable,<ref>Neumann</ref> so we can define <math>f(a+\varepsilon):=\sum \limits_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}\varepsilon^n</math>. This defines a ring homomorphism <math>\mathcal{A}_a \longrightarrow K\left[\left[T^\Gamma\right]\right]</math>.

== Hahn–Witt series ==

The construction of Hahn series can be combined with [[Witt vector]]s (at least over a [[perfect field]]) to form '''twisted Hahn series''' or '''Hahn–Witt series''':<ref>Kedlaya (2001, ''J. Number Theory'')</ref> for example, over a [[finite field]] ''K'' of characteristic ''p'' (or their algebraic closure), the field of Hahn–Witt series with value group ''Γ'' (containing the [[integer]]s) would be the set of formal sums <math>\sum_{e\in\Gamma} c_e p^e</math> where now <math>c_e</math> are [[Teichmüller representative]]s (of the elements of ''K'') which are multiplied and added in the same way as in the case of ordinary Witt vectors (which is obtained when ''Γ'' is the group of integers). When ''Γ'' is the group of rationals or reals and ''K'' is the algebraic closure of the finite field with ''p'' elements, this construction gives a (ultra)metrically complete algebraically closed field containing the [[p-adic number|''p''-adics]], hence a more or less explicit description of the field <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math> or its spherical completion.<ref>Poonen (1993)</ref>

==Examples==
* The field <math>K((T))</math> of [[formal Laurent series]] over <math>K</math> can be described as <math>K[[T^\mathbb Z]]</math>.
* The field of [[surreal number]]s can be regarded as a field of Hahn series with real coefficients and value group the surreal numbers themselves.<ref>Alling (1987)</ref>
* The [[Levi-Civita field]] can be regarded as a [[field extension|subfield]] of <math>\mathbb{R}[[T^\mathbb{Q}]]</math>, with the additional imposition that the coefficients be a [[left-finite set]]: the set of coefficients less than a given coefficient <math>c_q</math> is finite.
* The field of [[transseries]] <math>\mathbb{T}</math> is a directed union of Hahn fields (and is an extension of the Levi-Civita field).  The construction of <math>\mathbb{T}</math> resembles (but is not literally) <math>T_0 = \mathbb{R}</math>, <math>T_{n+1} = \mathbb{R}\left[\left[\varepsilon^{T_n}\right]\right]</math>.
